verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and none stops review at level 1 or 2. The goal extends the existing wal_compression setting, and the open points are fixable: the default and opt-out (standards-compat-1), the codec needed to read block references (replication-ondisk-1), and workload evidence (demand-1). The WAL record format change and the WIP streams rule (replication-ondisk-2) need a committer who knows xlogreader and recovery to sign.

brief.title: Compress whole WAL records above a size threshold
brief.problem: Today wal_compression compresses each full-page image on its own, so it cannot use redundancy shared by several images in one record, or between records. Large non-FPI records, such as 2PC records, are not compressed at all. The target is any cluster where WAL volume matters, with B-tree index builds as the main example.
brief.proposed_design: A record larger than wal_compression_threshold is compressed as one unit with lz4 or zstd, alongside per-FPI compression, and is marked by a spare xl_info bit plus a small header. If whole-record compression does not save space, the record falls back to per-FPI compression. A WIP patch keeps zstd history across records in a pool of streams that reset at fixed 4MB boundaries, so readers can start mid-WAL.
user_visible_surface: New GUC wal_compression_threshold, default 512 bytes, which sets the record size above which the whole record is compressed.
New GUC wal_compression_streams (WIP patch), a pool of compression streams that keep history across records.
WAL record format change: the XLR_COMPRESSED bit in xl_info and a compression header with method and decompressed length.
pg_waldump and pg_walinspect report physical record sizes separately from decoded sizes.
pg_stat_wal wal_fpi_bytes counts image bytes before whole-record compression, so it can exceed wal_bytes.
author_claims: CREATE INDEX over 10M random doubles writes 19% less WAL with zstd and 15% less with lz4.
Records below the threshold are unchanged, and each record still decodes on its own without streams.
Setting the threshold above the largest possible record restores today's behaviour.
Streams cut pgbench WAL per transaction by 17% to 37%, with a throughput cost between none and 12%.
A backend with whole-record compression enabled holds about twice the old compression buffer memory.
brief.thread_state: The zstd context reuse split out of this series was committed in two parts by Michael Paquier in October 2026. v13 of whole-record compression, the pg_walinspect change and WIP streams answers Zsolt Parragi's review and has no reply, and the buffer allocation question asked of Michael Paquier is still open.
unclear: The material gives no basis for the 512-byte default threshold beyond the author's intuition.
The material does not say whether the wal_compression_buffer GUC from v6 still exists in v13.
The material does not say how a standby or tool from an older release reacts to compressed records, or whether WAL page magic changes.
Surya Poondla's concern about page LSN and hint-only records got no visible answer, and may concern a different patch.
Parts of messages 16 and 17 are truncated, including the stream lock cost discussion.

objections.title: Gain for whole-record compression is shown on one synthetic workload only
objections.failure_scenario: A user turns on zstd with the default 512-byte threshold on an OLTP cluster and expects lower WAL volume. In that workload few records exceed the threshold, so the change in WAL volume is small. Meanwhile the record format change, the second compression buffer and the extra reader path are permanent for every release and every WAL tool.
objections.argument: The only measured benefit of 0002 is CREATE INDEX over 10M random doubles: 19% less WAL with zstd and 15% with lz4 (messages #4, #17). The 2PC case from message #1 has no numbers. No field report, -general thread or production WAL sample shows how much real WAL sits in large multi-FPI records. Michael Paquier committed the context-reuse parts but had no opinion on 0002 and 0003 (message #25), and the other interested reviewers (messages #6, #21) state liking the idea without giving a workload.
objections.author_must_show: On which production or realistic workloads, other than a B-tree build on random data, does 0002 reduce WAL volume, and by how much at the default threshold?

critic.reasoning: Message #16 shows records over 512 bytes hold 47.5% of pgbench WAL bytes, which weakens the "few records" scenario. But the only measured gain over per-FPI compression is the CREATE INDEX case, and no field report is shown.

objections.title: Default threshold turns on whole-record compression for every existing wal_compression user
objections.failure_scenario: A site runs wal_compression = on and upgrades. With the 512-byte default, large records are now compressed whole and need a second buffer per backend, and WAL size and CPU change. To get the old behaviour back, the DBA has to find a second GUC and set it to about 1GB.
objections.argument: In message #11 Fujii Masao asked to keep FPI-only compression as a real choice, and message #12 agreed to complement it. But the opt-out in message #13 is a magic threshold value, with no explicit setting. The 512 default has no measured basis (message #7), and message #16 shows a low threshold can make WAL larger. wal_compression already selects the method, so a committer would likely ask why the scope is not chosen there.
objections.author_must_show: Why is whole-record compression on by default for existing wal_compression users, and why is the opt-out a large threshold value with no explicit off setting?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 gives a 1GB threshold as the only way back to FPI-only compression, and message #7 gives no measured basis for 512. Message #35 spares FPI-only settings the new buffers, but lz4 and zstd users still get the new path by default.

objections.title: Whole-record compression hides block references behind the codec
objections.failure_scenario: A cluster runs with wal_compression = on, which now picks zstd first, so every record over 512 bytes is compressed as one unit. A pg_rewind binary, or an out-of-tree WAL reader built without zstd, can no longer parse the block headers of those records. It fails during a failover rewind or an incremental backup scan, not when the setting is changed.
objections.argument: Today a reader without lz4 or zstd can still decode record headers and block references and fails only on restoring an image. With 0002 the block headers sit inside the compressed payload (message #1), so codec support decides whether the record can be read at all. The default threshold turns this on for every existing wal_compression = lz4, zstd or on user, with no opt-in (messages #7, #20). The material also does not say whether XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC is bumped, so older tools may misread records instead of rejecting them (message #3).
objections.author_must_show: Why should whole-record compression be on by default for existing wal_compression users, and how does a reader without the codec report the problem instead of misparsing?

critic.reasoning: Message #18 quotes a "not supported by build" error, so a reader without the codec reports the problem and does not misparse. The narrower point stands: tools that need only block references now need the codec, by default.

objections.title: wal_fpi_bytes exceeding wal_bytes changes the meaning of a pg_stat_wal column
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring dashboard plots wal_fpi_bytes / wal_bytes as the full-page-image share of WAL. After upgrade the ratio goes above 1, as in message #33 (90 MB against 10 MB), and alerts or capacity plans built on it give wrong answers. Users learn of the change only from a release-notes line or the documentation.
objections.argument: Today wal_fpi_bytes is a subset of wal_bytes, and external tools depend on that. Message #35 keeps the pre-compression count, documents that it can exceed wal_bytes, and says the jointly compressed bytes cannot be split. That reason holds, but the result is one view whose two byte columns count in different units. A committer would likely ask for a separate column, or for wal_fpi_bytes to stay physical.
objections.author_must_show: Can pg_stat_wal keep wal_fpi_bytes no larger than wal_bytes, for example by reporting pre-compression image bytes in a new column instead?

critic.reasoning: Message #35 documents the change but does not keep the ratio that monitoring tools compute today. P2 must not be used as support, because its recorded reason argues against adding counters to pg_stat_wal.

objections.title: Two record lengths that every future xlogreader change must choose between
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a sanity check, a statistic or a buffer size based on xl_tot_len in xlogreader or pg_waldump. It is correct for uncompressed records, which is all the default test setup produces. With whole-record compression on, it checks or allocates the wrong side, and this shows up as a decode failure or a wrong report in the field.
objections.argument: 0002 splits each record into a physical length and a decoded length. Message #20 shows a rebase across 18992dc9d98 that needed a choice of side, and a plain textual rebase compiled against a variable that no longer existed. Message #36 found replorigin_identity reading xl_info without masking XLR_COMPRESSED. v13 clears the flag after decompression, but nothing makes the wrong choice of length fail loudly.
objections.author_must_show: Which test configuration runs the recovery and tool suites with whole-record compression on, so that a check on the wrong length fails in CI?

critic.reasoning: The series has a dedicated test, and message #14 shows v6 set lz4 for the recovery tests. The material does not say v13 keeps that setting, so the question about suite-wide coverage stands.

other_surviving.title: Stream mode depends on an unenforced rule about LSN-addressed reads
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch or an extension reads a record directly at a stored LSN, the way twophase.c reads PREPARE, without calling XLogBeginReadStreamed(). Its tests pass because wal_compression_streams is off by default. A user who turns streams on gets a record that refuses to decompress, possibly during recovery or commit of a prepared transaction.
other_surviving.argument: The rule for 0003 is a property: anything read by LSN without its predecessors must stay out of the streams. It is kept today by excluding checkpoint, PREPARE and XLOG_SWITCH records and by moving in-tree readers to XLogBeginReadStreamed() (messages #16, #17). The proposal does not make a new by-LSN reader or a new rmgr fail loudly when the rule is broken, and the default-off setting hides it from the test suite. A damaged record also makes the rest of its 4MB stream unreadable to salvage tools.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What check makes a direct-LSN read of a stream-compressed record fail in the default test runs, rather than only in clusters that enable streams?

critic.reasoning: Message #17 says such a record refuses to decompress, so the failure is loud at run time, but only in clusters with streams on. The material shows no check that catches a new by-LSN reader in default test runs.

refuted.title: Shared compression streams may leak other sessions' data through WAL size
refuted.failure_scenario: A superuser turns on wal_compression_streams. An unprivileged user inserts guessed values, such as token prefixes, and reads pg_current_wal_lsn() or pg_stat_wal before and after each insert. A guess that matches recent records written by another role into the same stream compresses better, so WAL grows less, and the guess is confirmed byte by byte on a quiet cluster.
refuted.argument: In 0003 a backend leases a stream from a shared pool and compresses each record against earlier records in that stream, including records other backends wrote (messages #16, #17, #35). That is the setup for a compression-ratio side channel: attacker-chosen input mixed with secret input, and the output length visible to the attacker. Per-FPI compression already mixes rows on one page, but streams widen the history to every role's records within a 4 MiB stretch. The thread does not discuss who can observe WAL growth or whether the stream history should be split by role.
refuted.author_must_show: How does 0003 stop an unprivileged role from learning another role's recent data by measuring WAL growth after inserts it controls?

critic.reasoning: Message #16 says a backend that takes over a lease restarts the stream, because compressor state is backend-local. Message #35 keeps one compressor per writer, so the material does not show a record compressed against another backend's records.

refuted.title: Streams make every future read-by-LSN path depend on an exclusion rule
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a feature that stores an LSN and reads that record directly, the way twophase.c reads a PREPARE record. The tests pass because wal_compression_streams is off by default. A production cluster with streams on then refuses to decompress the record, and the user finds out when that feature runs.
refuted.argument: Message #16 defines the exclusion rule as a property, not a list: anything read by LSN without replaying what comes before it must stay independent. Message #17 routes pg_waldump, pg_walinspect, logical decoding, walsummarizer and pg_rewind through XLogBeginReadStreamed(). Every new WAL consumer, in core or in an extension, must know this rule and use that call, and with streams off by default the tests do not catch a mistake. In message #25 the only engaged committer gave no opinion on 0003.
refuted.author_must_show: What makes a new WAL reader, or a new record read by stored LSN, fail in the regression suite when it ignores the stream rules?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-2, which states the same rule and scenario with the fitting severity. A missing test-time check in a WIP patch is fixable.

refuted.title: Existing wal_compression users get new memory and CPU costs by default
refuted.failure_scenario: A cluster with wal_compression = on, which now prefers zstd, upgrades. Every backend that writes a record over 512 bytes holds a second buffer of about 268 KiB and makes an extra compression attempt per large record. With many connections this adds hundreds of MiB, and the user sees it only as higher memory use and CPU.
refuted.argument: Message #17 says a backend with compression enabled holds about twice the old buffer memory. Message #16 says a low threshold can make WAL larger. The 512-byte default has no measurement behind it (message #7). Since 931c9701f25 made on mean zstd first (message #20), the new path becomes default for many users without a separate opt-in.
refuted.author_must_show: What measurements across workloads, including many-connection OLTP, support enabling whole-record compression at 512 bytes for everyone who sets wal_compression?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which already covers the default threshold, the second buffer and the CPU cost for existing wal_compression users. The request for many-connection measurements belongs with that objection.

refuted.title: Archive-side compression already captures cross-record redundancy for stored WAL
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator enables whole-record compression or streams to cut WAL storage. They already compress archived segments with an `archive_command` that pipes through gzip or zstd, or with a backup tool. The archive shrinks little further, but every backend now holds the extra buffer and every reader pays to decompress.
refuted.argument: The Postgres docs already describe compressing segments in `archive_command`, and whole-segment compression sees redundancy across all records, not only within one. That leaves local pg_wal write I/O and streaming replication bandwidth as the cases that archive compression cannot reach. The thread measures `wal_bytes` (messages #4, #17) but never says which of these volumes matters to users, or how much compression of archived segments already saves. For 0003 the overlap is larger, since it rebuilds stream state that segment compression gets at no cost.
refuted.author_must_show: Which cost does this reduce that compressing archived segments cannot: local WAL write I/O, replication bandwidth, or something else, and is there a measurement of it?

critic.reasoning: Compressing archived segments cannot reduce WAL written to pg_wal or sent to standbys, which is what the existing wal_compression setting targets. An operator who gains little from a setting they can raise or turn off is not a failure.

refuted.title: Archive-side compression already captures cross-record redundancy for stored WAL
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator whose main concern is archive size enables wal_compression_streams. Their archive_command already compresses whole segments, so the archive barely shrinks. They still pay up to 12% throughput at 64 clients, and pg_waldump, pg_rewind and logical decoding must now rewind to a 4MB stream reset point.
refuted.argument: Message #16 motivates 0003 by cross-record redundancy in small records. Compressing a whole WAL segment after it is written exploits that same redundancy for archive storage at no insert-path cost. What 0003 adds over that is lower local WAL writes and lower replication bandwidth. The material does not show users limited by either, while message #17 reports a throughput cost of up to 12% and a new reader rewind rule.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users are limited by local WAL write volume or replication bandwidth, in ways that segment compression at archive time does not already solve?

critic.reasoning: wal_compression_streams is off by default in a WIP patch, so the throughput cost and the reader rewind fall only on clusters that enable it. Item 4 fails when everyone pays, and the scenario describes an operator who opted in.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the XLR_COMPRESSED bit in xl_info and a compression header to the WAL record format.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch changes xlogrecord.h and xlogreader.h, and the streams patch adds XLogBeginReadStreamed() for WAL readers.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Default threshold turns on whole-record compression for every existing wal_compression user

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The series adds wal_compression_threshold and, in the WIP patch, wal_compression_streams.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Each record gets a physical and a decoded length, and streams add a rule for every reader that reads by LSN.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The WAL insert path in xloginsert.c gains a compression attempt and a second buffer per backend.

questions: On which realistic workloads, other than a B-tree build on random data, does whole-record compression reduce WAL volume at the 512-byte default, and by how much?
Why is whole-record compression on by default for existing lz4 and zstd users, with a large threshold value as the only way back to FPI-only compression?
Which in-tree tools and known out-of-tree WAL readers need only block references today, and how do they behave on a compressed record when built without the codec?
Can pg_stat_wal keep wal_fpi_bytes no larger than wal_bytes, for example by reporting image bytes before compression in a new column?
Which test configuration runs the recovery and tool suites with whole-record compression on, and with streams on, so a wrong length or a direct read by LSN fails in CI?

committability.owner_note: Michael Paquier committed the zstd context reuse split out of this series, but in message #25 gave no opinion on whole-record compression or streams. The owner must know xloginsert, xlogreader and recovery.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a WAL record format change read by recovery, standbys, pg_rewind, pg_waldump, logical decoding and out-of-tree readers, for every later release. With streams, the owner also signs for the rule on records read by LSN.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has posted 13 versions since January 2025, rebased across seven CommitFests and answered the latest review in v13.

priority.reason: Users of wal_compression with lz4 or zstd gain, with 15% to 19% less WAL shown on one index build. The patch changes the WAL record format and the insert and reader paths, so the default, the opt-out and the pg_stat_wal meaning should be settled before detailed review.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check that every reader masks XLR_COMPRESSED and uses the right length, or whether the page magic changes. The truncated messages #16 and #17 hide the stream lock cost.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generic WAL compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes generic WAL record construction so that it can compute a minimal edit-distance delta between the old and new page images (using an O(ND) difference algorithm), and falls back to the existing bytewise-difference approach when the result is not short enough. The goal is to shrink generic WAL records for access methods such as RUM, where small insertions or deletions shift page contents and make the existing delta nearly page-sized.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch received only limited review across several commitfests. David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it still needed review and did not seem a good fit for the last commitfest of PG11. Open points from the visible review included the author's own finding of a large time overhead in one RUM case, and the request to make compression optional, which the author was still working on. Stephen Frost suggested resubmitting for a post-11 commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since the feature does not seem like a good fit for the last CF of PG11
I am marking it Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Tracking the compression effect
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add two cumulative columns to the pg_stat_wal view: bytes saved by WAL compression (size before minus size after) and the number of times compression ran. Users could then compare compression methods such as lz4 and zstd without running pg_waldump.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers preferred to report compression savings in pg_waldump and pg_walinspect, because WAL records already carry the saved-bytes information. Collecting the counters in pg_stat_wal would add code to every WAL record insert. The author agreed to switch to the pg_waldump and pg_walinspect approach, and the pg_stat_wal entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Collecting them in the server via pg_stat_wal
will require some extra effort, for instance, every WAL record insert
requires that code to be executed.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_receivewal fail to streams when the partial file to write is not fully initialized present in the wal receiver directory
precedents_retrieved.summary: pg_receivewal fails to start when a leftover .partial segment is not fully zero-padded, for example after ENOSPC or a VM crash, so the user must delete the file by hand. The patch writes and pads a new segment under a temporary name, then renames it to the .partial name, and removes any leftover temporary file on the next call.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry stalled. After v9 in October 2022 no reviewer responded for more than 15 months, so Peter Smith returned it with feedback, citing low interest. Earlier, Michael Paquier said the fix does nothing for gzip or lz4 segments and that the real need is to reserve disk space for a full segment. He also asked why a temporary file is needed when the .partial file already serves that role. The visible messages do not show whether v9 answered these points.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since there seems not much interest, I have changed the status to "Returned with Feedback" [1].

precedents_retrieved.summary: Compression dictionaries

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_receivewal fail to streams when the partial file to write is not fully initialized present in the wal receiver directory
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the zero-padding of a new WAL segment in pg_receivewal atomic by padding a XXXX.partial.tmp file and then renaming it to XXXX.partial, durably when sync is on. A crash or ENOSPC during padding would then not leave a short .partial file that blocks restart until someone removes it by hand.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said the temporary file only covers uncompressed segments, so gzip and lz4 segments can still fail midway, and that the real need is to reserve enough disk space before starting a segment. He also asked why a temporary file is needed when the .partial file already serves that role. Kyotaro Horiguchi preferred to error out with a hint to remove the bad file. The thread stops with these points open, and the visible messages do not show why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So the important part is not the pre-padding, it is to make sure that there is enough space reserved for the handling of a full segment before beginning the work on it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical insert/update/delete WAL records for custom table AMs
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add new WAL records representing a logical insert, update, delete (and later truncate) that do nothing at REDO time and are only processed during logical decoding, so that custom table AMs such as a columnar extension can support logical decoding/replication without extensible WAL. Later versions added SQL functions pg_logical_emit_insert/update/delete/truncate and tests using test_decoding.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch, saying that with custom WAL resource managers (his parallel extensible rmgr work) it had become less important to him. Earlier, Amit Kapila questioned whether a common heap-tuple-based format could work for all table AMs, and the patch had stopped applying, but the visible messages show no deciding objection from a reviewer.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Withdrawn for now. With custom WAL resource managers this is less
important to me.

precedents_retrieved.title: Move walreceiver state assignment (to WALRCV_STREAMING) in WalReceiverMain()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the assignment of walrcv->walRcvState to WALRCV_STREAMING from the start of WalReceiverMain() to the point after walrcv_startstreaming() returns true. The author said the current placement causes no known issue but is less accurate, since connecting to the primary can still fail after it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Euler Taveira was concerned that keeping the state at WALRCV_STARTING longer could let WalRcvStreaming() hit the hardcoded WALRCV_STARTUP_TIMEOUT and stop a walreceiver that is slow to connect. Michael Paquier agreed and noted that v1 skipped the restart case. The author fixed the restart case in v2, but CFbot then reported test failures, and he withdrew the patch because the current code causes no issues.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Couldn't it give up before starting if you apply your patch? My main concern is
due to a slow system, the walrcv_connect() took to long in WalReceiverMain()
and the code above kills the walreceiver while in the process to start it.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_basebackup: add test about zstd compress option
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a test to pg_basebackup's TAP tests that exercises the zstd compression option, later extended to verify the generated files with the zstd binary. A follow-up version refactored the test to cover multiple compression methods (gzip, lz4, zstd) and check output with each respective decompression program.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas pointed out that existing tests in src/bin/pg_verifybackup (008_untar.pl and 009_extract.pl) already cover compressed base backups, and that the only additional scenario the new test could catch was not worth the extra CPU cycles. Ian Lawrence Barwick and the author agreed the test did not add anything, and the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I would be inclined to dismiss that particular scenario as not important
enough to be worth the additional CPU cycles.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P1] is a delta format for generic WAL and was returned for lack of review time, and [P2] proposed pg_stat_wal counters, which this proposal does not add. [P4] and [P10] record no reason. The thread cites only a related wal_compression default discussion (messages #17 and #28), not an earlier attempt at whole-record compression.
The WAL format change itself is not objected to: WAL is tied to a major version, and standbys and pg_upgrade do not carry WAL across versions. The WIP streams GUC was not judged.
0002 keeps each record decodable on its own and leaves pg_upgrade and the catalog unchanged. The page LSN concern in message #21 seems to concern another patch, so it was not used.

0002 alone adds little new exposure: records stay independent, and message #20 caps the decompressed length at XLogRecordMaxSize. The GUC contexts for the new settings are not shown, so I could not check who can set them.
The context-reuse part is committed. These objections apply to 0002 and 0003 only.

Only one objection from this angle. Per-FPI wal_compression cannot use redundancy across images, and core has no compression of the replication stream, so no existing feature fully replaces the proposal.
Interest in lower WAL volume is broad, and wal_compression already exists. The objections ask for workload evidence, not a rejection.
